CPESR Exam 4 — Compiled Review

55 questions, transcribed + tagged from the image-based source, matching Exam 1/2/3 format.

Q1. Which of the following GPS surveying techniques is the most precise?
Igis
  • A) RTK
  • B) Pseudo-Static
  • C) Static
  • D) Pseudo-Kinematic
RTK is real time kinematic and refers to a stop-and-go method in which the coordinates of points are available in real time. In this method, a radio communication link is maintained between the base and the rover. This method is used for most operations that do not require the highest order of accuracy. Static refers to a method that requires the highest order of precision. It is also the slowest form of collecting data. Pseudo-Kinematic and Pseudo-Static are the same thing and are a combination of both static and kinematic methods. They have the speed of the kinematic method but do not need to maintain lock on 4 satellites. They are the least precise of all methods.

Answer: C
Q2. A distance in the field was very carefully measured twice and two distinctly separate readings were recorded in the field book. Later in the office, the two readings were shown to be slightly different. This difference is called a
Itheory
  • A) Discrepancy error
  • B) Accidental error
  • C) Resultant error
  • D) Systematic error
The observed difference itself is a "discrepancy," but the question is asking what TYPE of error is responsible for it. Since the measurement was taken very carefully both times and the readings still differ slightly (rather than showing a consistent, repeatable bias like a systematic error, or a large mistake like a blunder), the cause is accidental (random) error — small, unpredictable variations inherent to any measurement.

Answer: B
Q3. The bearing and distance of line SR is
IIItrav

  • A) N71°15'43"E, 1227.12'
  • B) S41°25'12"W, 1888.28'
  • C) S18°44'17"W, 1551.25'
  • D) S71°15'43"W, 1551.25'
Latitude/departure from P to Q: sin 28°19'49"(1325.73) = 629.13 = x cos 28°19'49"(1325.73) = −1166.94 = y Latitude/departure from Q to R: sin 21°32'31"(674.54) = 247.68 = x cos 21°32'31"(674.54) = 627.42 = y Coordinates at R: y = 774.90 − 1166.94 + 627.42 = 235.38 x = 1143.21 + 629.13 + 247.68 = 2020.02 R(235.38, 2020.02) Distance SR: Distance = √[(3489.05−2020.02)² + (733.71−235.38)²] = 1551.25 ft Since this problem figure is to scale, you could stop here knowing that the azimuth of line SR is closer to 270 degrees than 180 degrees. This means the bearing must be a larger degree to the west — probably closer to South 71 degrees West than South 18 degrees West — but here is the rest of the calculation: θ = tan⁻¹(\(\dfrac{x}{y}\)) = tan⁻¹[\(\dfrac{(3489.05-2020.02)}{(733.71-235.38)}\)] θ = 71°15'43" = S71°15'43"W

Answer: D
Q4. The DMD method is used to
IIItrav
  • A) balance a closed traverse
  • B) compute areas of closed traverses
  • C) balance angles
  • D) balance an open traverse
The Double Meridian Distance Method is used to calculate area.

Answer: B
Q5. A steel 100 foot tape was used to measure a slope distance of 376.13 ft on a 3% slope. The tape is fully standardized at 68°F and supported under a tension of 12 lbs. Tape cross sectional area = 0.006 square inches. Elastic modulus = 29,000,000 lb/square inches. If the tape was laid on the ground with a pull of 29 lbs at temperature 33°F, the true slope distance is
IIdist
  • A) 375.91 ft
  • B) 376.01 ft
  • C) 376.08 ft
  • D) 375.84 ft
Sign conventions: increased tension shortens the effective tape length, so the measured distance reads short and needs a (+) correction. Decreased temperature also shortens the tape, so the measured distance reads long and needs a (−) correction. Temperature correction: C_temperature = (\(\dfrac{0.00000645}{\text{\textdegree}F}\))(T − T₀)(L_measured) = (0.00000645)(33 − 68)(376.13) C_temperature = −0.085 Tension correction: C_tension = \(\dfrac{(P - P_{0})(L_{\text{measured}})}{(AE)}\) = \(\dfrac{(29 - 12)(376.13)}{[(0.006)(2.9 \times 10^{7})]}\) C_tension = 0.037 True slope distance: 376.13 − 0.085 + 0.037 = 376.08 ft
Instructor clarification (from a comment thread): this is a measurement question, not a layout question — the way to tell is that the question isn't asking you to lay out a previously-known distance; it's just describing how a measurement was made, with the details spread throughout the question. If it had instead described a distance measured at one time, then asked you to reproduce it under different conditions (e.g. different temperature and tension), that would be a layout problem instead.

Answer: C
Q6. Determine the coordinates of point B.
IIItrav
  • A) N1089.13, E803.12
  • B) N1133.23, E778.45
  • C) N1102.89, E809.67
  • D) N1112.58, E830.86
Create triangle BCD to find the length of BC: \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)\) \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1056.04-901.58}{958.22-937.40}\right)\) θ = 82°19'24" Bearing CD = 82°19'24" = N82°19'24"E Distance CD = \(\sqrt{(1056.04-901.58)^2+(958.22-937.40)^2}\) Distance CD = 155.86 ft ∠BCD = N21°59'1"W + N82°19'24"E ∠BCD = 104°18'25" Law of Sine: \(\dfrac{\sin 104°18'25"}{273} = \dfrac{\sin ∠CBD}{155.86}\) ∠CBD = 33°35'15" ∠CDB = 180° − 104°18'25" − 33°35'15" ∠CDB = 42°6'20" \(\dfrac{\sin 104°18'25"}{273} = \dfrac{\sin 42°6'20"}{BC}\) BC = 188.91 ft Find the x and y component of line BC then add to the northing/easting of point C: Δy = 188.91 cos 21°59'1" = 175.175 Δx = 188.91 sin 21°59'1" = 70.717 Northing B = 937.40 + 175.175 = 1112.58 Easting B = 901.58 − 70.717 = 830.86
Note: this is a very long problem — attempt it only after the easier questions, or if you know you have plenty of time. The central angle (Δ = 37°) shown in the figure is a decoy and is not needed for this solution path.

Answer: D
Q7. If the clearance between the FG of the roadway (not including the 2-foot gutter) and the top of the 18" SD pipe is a minimum of 3', what is the highest invert elevation at the bottom of the 18" SD as shown?
Vconstr
  • A) 325.00'
  • B) 325.09'
  • C) 326.80'
  • D) 324.60'
Elevation of FG above the high point of 18" SD: 330.50 − (20 − 2)(0.02) = 330.14' Max elevation at top of 18" SD at high point: 330.14 − 3 = 327.14' Max elevation at top of 18" SD at low point: 327.14 − (21)(0.016) = 326.80' Max elevation at the invert of 18" SD at the low point: 326.80' − \(\dfrac{2.5}{12}\) − \(\dfrac{18}{12}\) = 325.09'
Note: make sure you memorize or can easily recall the legend — its contents are common on the exam and in practice.

Answer: B
Q8. A highway centerline begins at Point A which is the BC of a curve. Point A is due south of the radius point with a radius of 1000 feet. The curve concaves up and ends at Point B which is the PRC and northeast of Point A. Then the reverse curve starts at Point B concaving down and ends at Point C (EC of curve) at station 104+00. The radius point of curve BC is to the south with a radius of 600 feet. Thence a straight tangent to Point D at station 109+00. The bearing of CD is S75°E and Point D is directly east of Point A. The highway is proposed to move to a new location which is the straight line between Points A and D. What is the length of the new alignment AD?
Vhc
  • A) 1296.69 ft
  • B) 1209.58 ft
  • C) 1088.97 ft
  • D) 1314.33 ft
Draw a quick sketch. The key is to identify the radius distances and use the given information to find the horizontal distance. Length AD = X + Y + Z: GA = GB = 1000' GF = GB + BF = 1000 + 600 = 1600' CD = (109+00) − (104+00) = 5+00 = 500' X = DO    Y = OH    Z = HA = FE Find X distance — find angle D then use triangle DCO: Angle D = 90 − 75 = 15° X = \(\dfrac{CD}{\cos 15°}\) X = \(\dfrac{500}{\cos 15°}\) = 517.638' Find Y distance — find CO, then subtract from radius CF to find OF, then use triangle OFH: CO = CD tan 15° = 500(tan 15°) = 133.975' OF = 600 − CO = 466.025' Y = OF sin 15° = 466.025(sin 15°) = 120.616' Find Z distance — use triangle OFH to find FH, add to GA, then use triangle GFE: FH = OF cos 15° = 466.025(cos 15°) = 450.146' FH = AE GE = GA + AE = 1000 + 450.146 = 1450.146' Z = \(\sqrt{GF^2 - GE^2}\) Z = \(\sqrt{1600^2 - 1450.146^2}\) = 676.076' Find length AD by adding X + Y + Z: Length AD = X + Y + Z = 517.638 + 120.616 + 676.076 = 1314.33'
Note: PRC is the point of reverse curve — the point where two curves join.

Answer: D

Q10. A new park will be constructed in a developing rural area. The developer has been given a set of complete design plans to construct a lake near the steepest area of the park. What type of surveying is needed to construct the lake?
Vconstr
  • A) Hydrographic Surveying
  • B) Aerial Surveying
  • C) Construction Surveying
  • D) Topographic Surveying
Since the developer already has a complete set of design plans, the lake has already been designed — what remains is staking out that design in the field, which is Construction Surveying.
Note: "Yes that is correct. If the project were not designed yet, a topographic survey would be needed." — Instructor Kirk T.

Answer: C
Q11. A proposed highway has a 50 ft width and the following profile. The total quantity of material added or removed between sta 48+00 and sta 50+00 is approximately
Varea
  • A) 2431 yd³ cut
  • B) 2019 yd³ cut
  • C) 1375 yd³ cut
  • D) 2906 yd³ cut
There is no time to calculate this exactly; we need to approximate by breaking it down into triangles and rectangles. Since this is to scale, Area 1 can be approximated with the rectangle shown to cover all the area in that region. Remember that the goal is always to come up with a single unique answer so approximations like this will work when the answers are spread out. \(area\ 1 = 2.5 \times 25 = 62.5\ ft^2\ cut\ area\) \(area\ 2 = \dfrac{15\times75}{2} = 562.5\ ft^2\ cut\ area\) \(area\ 3 = \dfrac{10\times100}{2} = 500\ ft^2\ cut\ area\) \(area\ 4 = \dfrac{5\times100}{2} = 250\ ft^2\ cut\ area\) \(\sum = 1375\ ft^2\ cut\ area\) \(\dfrac{1375\ ft^2\times50\ ft}{27\ ft^3/yd^3} = 2546\ yd^3\) \(actual\ answer = 2431\ yd^3\)

Answer: A
Q12. What is the approximate volume of excavation necessary to construct the pad if the pad elevation is 200? (pad is shaded)
Varea
  • A) 530 cu yd
  • B) 780 cu yd
  • C) 465 cu yd
  • D) 930 cu yd
Assume uniform, linear change between elevations. The pad is at elevation 200. From the shaded pad's cross section A-A, the ground rises from elevation 200 to elevation 205 over the 50 ft width of the pad: Volume = \(\left(\dfrac{50 \times 5}{2}\right)\) × 100 Volume = 12,500 ft³ = 462.96 yd³ = 465 yd³

Answer: C

Q14. A rod reading on a benchmark is 7.85. If the angle of the plumb bob, attached to the rod at rod reading 7.85, is 14°, the elevation of the benchmark in relation to the base of the level instrument with HI=5.23 is
IIlevel
  • A) +2.62 ft
  • B) −2.62 ft
  • C) −1.90 ft
  • D) −2.39 ft
The rod is tilted 14° off vertical (leaning away from plumb), so the true (vertical) reading is the horizontal projection of the 7.85 rod length: \(\cos 14° = \dfrac{x}{7.85}\) x = 7.62 ft HI = 5.23, FS = 7.62 5.23 − 7.62 = −2.39 ft

Answer: D
Q15. A dirt path is to be graded for paving. The path has a 75-foot R/W width with a proposed road width of 35 feet and up to a 1:1 max side slopes. The cost of embankment is $100 per cubic yard and the cost for cut is $150 per cubic yard. Assuming uniform change in elevation, the cost of only excavation for the stretch shown below is?
Varea
StationExisting ElevProposed Elev
17+007080
18+008585
19+0090100
20+00110110
21+0011595
  • A) $610,000
  • B) $1,220,000
  • C) $305,000
  • D) $455,000
R/W stands for right of way, the area owned by an entity. The full width of the R/W is 75 ft, which remains constant. The only excavation in the table is between station 20+00 and 21+00, where existing elevation is higher than proposed elevation. Since there is no cut or fill at station 20+00 (even ground), we can use the average-end-area method to find the volume. The cross-sectional area of the trench shape is found by averaging the top and bottom width, times height: V = L(\(\dfrac{A_1+A_2}{2}\)) bottom of roadway width = 35 top of R/W width = 35 + 20 + 20 = 75 height = 115 − 95 = 20 V = 100(\(\dfrac{0+\frac{35+75}{2}(20)}{2}\)) V = 550(100) ft³ V = 55,000 ft³ = 2037.04 yd³ 2037.04 yd³ × $150 per yd³ = $305,556

Answer: C
Q16. In a closed traverse, theoretically, the sum of the backsights and the sum of the foresights equals
IIItrav
  • A) the same absolute value
  • B) an arbitrary number
  • C) zero
  • D) three times the value of the backsights
A closed traverse is properly surveyed if the backsights and foresights are equal. This would mean there is no error in the calculation and surveying process.

Answer: A
Q17. A vertical sag curve has a rising grade of 4.6% and a falling grade of 3.5%. The lowest point is 425 ft from the PVC. The distance from the lowest point to the PVT is
Vvc
  • A) 9.84 sta
  • B) 5.59 sta
  • C) 3.23 sta
  • D) 7.48 sta
Find length of curve using the low point equation: \(D_o = \dfrac{LG}{G-G\prime}\) 4.25 = \(\dfrac{L(-3.5)}{-3.5-4.6}\) L = 9.84 sta Distance from low point to PVT: 9.84 − 4.25 = 5.59 sta

Answer: B
Q18. A side slope of a wide trench is to be constructed on flat land. At what station is the catch point?
Vconstr
Station7+739+0610+7112+13
Elevation161.44174.74191.24205.44
Existing elevation along this stretch (dashed reference line): 183.74
  • A) 9+81
  • B) 9+96
  • C) 8+16
  • D) 11+23
Catch point is where the proposed meets the existing, and is therefore a location where the grade changes. We must interpolate at what station the elevation of the trench will reach the existing ground elevation (183.74): \(\dfrac{Rise}{Run} = \dfrac{191.24-174.74}{10+71-9+06} = \dfrac{16.5}{165} = 0.1 = 10\%\) 183.74 − 174.74 = 9 \(\dfrac{9}{x} = 0.1\) x = 90 90 + 906 = 996 = 9+96

Answer: B

Q21. If the final mass ordinate is less than the initial mass ordinate,
Varea
  • A) the elevation at the final point is lower than the initial point
  • B) the elevation at the final point is higher than the initial point
  • C) additional material must be obtained
  • D) there is an excess of excavation
The mass ordinate is the cumulative total of excavation minus embankment up to that point on the mass diagram. If the final ordinate is lower than the initial ordinate (the zero point), the project ends in a net fill condition, meaning additional material must be brought in.
Student/instructor discussion:
J.J.Mar 15
(original comment text not legible in source screenshot)
Instructor Kirk TMar 21
It is the point on the mass diagram that represents the cumulative total of the excavation and embankment up to that point. So if the ordinate is lower (on the y axis) than the initial ordinate (the zero point), then we are in a fill condition and material must be imported in.
N.C.May 04
How are the 2nd and 3rd options not the same? An excess of excavation means "fill" condition. Additional material must be obtained also means "fill" condition. Can you please explain?
Instructor Kirk TMay 29
It is actually the opposite. Excess of excavation means that there is too much excavation, which is the same as cut. Therefore these two options are not the same.

Answer: C

Dividing a large parcel into 5 or more parcels is done on a subdivision map.

Q23. The retired space shuttle Endeavour will be moved to a new location by way of surface streets. To do this, a path must be planned that has enough space to move the space shuttle on the roadway without causing damage. What is the largest clearance between the bridge and the roadway if the BVC is 40 feet below the bridge and the elevation of the PVI is 500 feet?
Vvc
  • A) 46 feet
  • B) 58 feet
  • C) 50 feet
  • D) 54 feet
The lowest point on the curve will provide the largest gap for the space shuttle to go through. \(elev_{BVC} = elev_{PVI} - G_1\dfrac{L}{2}\) \(elev_{BVC} = 500ft + 4\%\dfrac{900}{2} = 518ft\) \(D_o = \dfrac{LG_1}{G_1-G_2}\) \(D_o = \dfrac{(9sta)(-4\%)}{-4\%-(+3\%)} = 5.1429\ stations\) \(elev_{lowpoint} = elev_{BVC} + G_1x + \left(\dfrac{G_2-G_1}{2L}\right)x^2\) \(elev_{lowpoint} = 518ft - 4\%(5.1429sta) + \left(\dfrac{3\%-(-4\%)}{2(9sta)}\right)(5.1429sta)^2\) \(elev_{lowpoint} = 507.71ft\) \(Largest\ Clearance = elev_{BVC} + 40ft - elev_{lowpoint}\) \(Largest\ Clearance = 518ft + 40ft - 507.71ft = 50.29ft\)

Answer: C

Q25. A surveyor measures a vertical angle of 49°40'52" to the top of a hill, point B, from his set up point, point A. The height of the instrument is 4.72 ft. The elevation of point A is 573.82 ft. The coordinates of point HI and point B are as follows.

\((x, y) \text{ coordinates of } HI = (123.73,\ 514.13)\)
\((x, y) \text{ coordinates of } B = (357.14,\ 789.17)\)

The elevation of point B is
vc
  • A) 1003.61 ft
  • B) 853.58 ft
  • C) 685.26 ft
  • D) 690.26 ft
\(AB = \sqrt{(123.73 - 357.14)^2 + (514.13 - 789.17)^2}\) \(AB = 360.73 \text{ ft} = \text{Horizontal distance from A to B}\) \(360.73(\tan 49^\circ40'52") + 573.82 + 4.72 = 1003.61 \text{ ft}\)
Note: If you chose 853.58 as your answer, you are probably confusing the x–y plane with the z-coordinate. The coordinates are in the x–y plane but we are looking for the elevation which is a z-coordinate. The figure is viewed in the profile view. The 360.73 is the adjacent side which would be in the x–y-coordinate plane. Thus using the given coordinates, we can find the horizontal distance from A to B.

Answer: A
Q26. Given the plan shown below, what would be the largest horizontal scale on the profile sheet for the E–W stationing that includes all 4 MHs if the plans are printed on 24"x36" paper with 1" margins starting at station 0+00?

constr
  • A) 1"=20'
  • B) 1"=25'
  • C) 1"=15'
  • D) 1"=10'
To find the horizontal scale, find the distance from Manhole 1 to Manhole 4. Since Manhole 4 does not have a station number, estimate it using the plan with full station markings. \(\text{estimated location of } MH4 = 5 + 20 \text{ sta}\) \(\text{min horizontal length} = 520 \text{ ft}\) \(\text{printable area} = 36 - 1 - 1 = 34"\) \(\text{horizontal scale} = \dfrac{520 \text{ ft}}{34} = 15.29 \approx 1": 15.29'\) The scale technically needs to show the full manhole width, requiring a smaller scale to fit more horizontal length, which would be 1":20'. If the location of MH4 were assumed to be at 5+10, the scale would be 1":15'. However, that would place MH1 and MH4 at the edge of the printable area, likely illegible. Therefore the largest possible scale that should be used is 1":20'.
Note: A plan and profile sheet has two parts. The top half has a grid for showing elevation and distance, and the bottom shows the project in plan view. Features that require showing elevation, such as pipelines and roadway elevations, use this format.

Answer: A
Q27. In laying out a highway for construction, a cut beginning at sta 11+78.45 is necessary until the existing ground elevation matches the proposed elevation. The proposed elevation is 356.42 ft. The existing ground elevation at sta 11+78.45 is 371.13 ft. If the 3:1 cut slope is to be implemented along the centerline, the station at the catchpoint is
constr
  • A) 11+83.35
  • B) 11+73.55
  • C) 12+22.58
  • D) 11+93.16
\(371.13 - 356.42 = 14.71 \text{ ft elevation change}\) \(\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{14.71}{x}\) \(x = 44.13 \text{ ft}\) \(11+78.45 + 0+44.13 = 12+22.58\)
Note: Remember 3:1 slope in the English system (in, ft) is horizontal:vertical for surveying. Also remember that the catchpoint is where elevations meet.

Answer: C
Q28. Which one of the following does not affect the measurement of a GPS survey?
gis
  • A) Dilution of Precision
  • B) Rain
  • C) Refraction
  • D) Electromagnetic interference
The only one of these choices that has virtually no impact on the accuracy of GPS measurements is rain. Weather typically does not cause GPS errors unless there is rapid weather change, which is very unlikely. The others can affect GPS, however countermeasures can be taken to inhibit the errors. Electromagnetic interference can interfere with the operation of the GPS device. There are two types of refraction (ionosphere and troposphere) that are some of the largest errors. Dilution of Precision (DOP) is when all the satellites are too close to each other, which can also cause an error.

Answer: B
Q29. The San Gabriel Valley project will use the parameters in the following table. What will be the contour interval for this project?
San Gabriel Valley
Photogrammetry Project
Format:9 inch x 9 inch
End Lap:60%
Side Lap:30%
Photo Scale:1:3000
Height Above Datum:2,500 ft
Camera Focal Length:6 inches
C-Factor:750
Camera Type:Reseau

gis
  • A) 20
  • B) 2
  • C) 5
  • D) 3.3
Find the flight height above terrain. \(\dfrac{1}{3000} = 1": 250'\) \(\text{Photo scale} = \dfrac{f}{H - h}\) \(\dfrac{1"}{250'} = \dfrac{6"}{2500 - h}\) \(\dfrac{1"}{250'} = \dfrac{1"}{\frac{2500-h}{6}}\) \(250' = \dfrac{2500 - h}{6}\) \(h = 1000'\) \(\therefore \text{Flight height above terrain} = H - h = 2500 - 1000 = 1500'\) Find the contour interval. \(\text{C-factor} = \dfrac{\text{Flight height above terrain}}{\text{contour interval}}\) \(CI = \dfrac{\text{Flight height above terrain}}{\text{C-factor}} = \dfrac{1500}{750} = 2\)
Student/instructor discussion:
J.N.Mar 27
I get confused when to convert the focal length to feet for these type of problems. Is it always or what is a rule of thumb when to convert? When scale is given 1:3000 instead of 1"=250'?
Instructor Kirk TJul 30
The standard notation for focal length is inches to feet (e.g. 1"=250'). More often than not, this is the notation you will be using.

But you can always keep it in 1:3000 equivalent form as well. This would just be inch to inch in this case, so as long as you keep track of the units in the equation, you will ultimately simplify the equation to the point where you will eventually need to convert to a common unit, typically inch to feet. So you might as well keep it that way from the beginning.

Answer: B
Q30. A ground scale 325' x 500' rectangular lot is to be plotted on a 24" x 36" topographic survey. The margin on the paper is 1" on all sides. The signature block is 4" x 8" on the lower right corner in the standard 2x3 plan location. What is the largest scale that can be used for the lot?
area
  • A) 1":20'
  • B) 1":30'
  • C) 1":25'
  • D) 1":15'
To determine the scale that can be used, evaluate the x and y direction and pick a scale that works in both directions. First consider the scale with no signature block, subtracting the 1" margin from each side. \(Vertical scale = \dfrac{325}{22} = 14.77\) \(Horizontal scale = \dfrac{500}{34} = 14.71\) \(\therefore 1": 15'\) However, there is a signature block that will interfere with the plotting of the rectangular lot. We must subtract this area to find a scale that will work. \(Vertical scale = \dfrac{325}{18} = 18.06\) \(Horizontal scale = \dfrac{500}{26} = 19.23\) \(\therefore 1": 20' \text{ is sufficient}\)

Answer: A
Q31. The most common elevation datum for surveyors today is
level
  • A) NAD 83
  • B) NGVD 29
  • C) CCS83
  • D) NAVD 88
NAD 83 and CCS83 are the same and are horizontal datums. NGVD 29 is the old vertical datum.

Answer: D
Q32. A developer is interested in building a shopping center in the region shaded below. The developer must stay within the confines of the allotted area. There must also be a 150' setback from railroad tracks, a 250' setback from schools, and a 300' setback from bodies of water. The railroad and the river are parallel to each other. What is the maximum build area?

area
  • A) 81.23 acres
  • B) 110.42 acres
  • C) 108.59 acres
  • D) 76.27 acres
Since we have two parallel base lines, use the trapezoid area equation. Offset the top line by 150' and the bottom line by 300'. First calculate more information. Circle A: \(PO = \dfrac{150}{\tan 64^\circ1'28"} = 73.08'\) \(PQ = \dfrac{150}{\sin 64^\circ1'28"} = 166.86'\) Circle B \(SY = 300(\tan 25^\circ58'32") = 146.16'\) \(ST = \dfrac{300}{\cos 25^\circ58'32"} = 333.71'\) Circle C \(EX = \dfrac{150}{\tan 66^\circ4'38"} = 66.54'\) Circle D \(VZ = 300(\tan 23^\circ55'22") = 133.08'\) Find base 1, base 2, and the height of the allowable trapezoid area \(SV = 1604.76 + 146.16 + 133.08 = 1884.00\) \(QW = 3259.57 - 73.08 - 66.54 = 3119.95\) \(QS = 1977.59 - 166.86 - 333.71 = 1477.02\) \(\text{height} = 1477.02(\sin 64^\circ1'28") = 1327.81'\) \(\text{area of trapezoid} = \dfrac{b_1 + b_2}{2}(h) = \dfrac{1884.00 + 3119.95}{2}(1327.81)\) \(\text{area of trapezoid} = 3322147 \text{ ft}^2\) \(\text{area of trapezoid} = \dfrac{3322147}{43560} = 76.27 \text{ acres}\)

Answer: D
Q33. Given a curve between points A and C (curve right of ABC), what is the shortest distance between the curve and point D? Assume BD bisects ADC.

trav
  • A) 425.50'
  • B) 926.22'
  • C) 574.29'
  • D) 710.22'
Solve for E on the horizontal curve. Add it to line BD. Line BD is perpendicular to the curve. \(I = 180 - 132 = 48\) \(E = T\tan\dfrac{I}{4} = 700\tan\dfrac{48}{4}\) \(E = 148.79\) \(\text{Angle } C = 180^\circ - 67 - 89 = 24^\circ\) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\text{Angle } D = \dfrac{84}{2} \text{ or } 180^\circ - 90 - (24 + 24) = 42\) \(\dfrac{\sin C}{BD} = \dfrac{\sin D}{BC}\) \(\dfrac{\sin 24^\circ}{BD} = \dfrac{\sin 42^\circ}{700}\) \(BD = 425.50\) \(E + BD = 148.79 + 425.50\) \(E + BD = 574.29\)

Answer: C
Q34. Which of the following can Civil Engineers registered after January 1, 1982 do?
I
  • A) Establish easement
  • B) Property line for location of a retaining
  • C) None of these
  • D) Final map for right of way
Civil engineers registered after January 1, 1982 cannot do any of these tasks. They are reserved for land surveyors or civil engineers registered prior to January 1, 1982.

Answer: C
Q35. A concrete channel is to be constructed. What is the total volume of concrete needed between these two stations?

constr
  • A) 430 CY
  • B) 1130 CY
  • C) 950 CY
  • D) 1720 CY
Find the area of the trapezoids then remove the rectangular area, Sta 2+35. \(\text{Top of trapezoid} = 4 + 1 + 15 + 1 + 4 = 25\) \(\text{Bottom of trapezoid} = 1 + 15 + 1 = 17\) \(\text{Area}_{Trapezoid} = \dfrac{(a+b)h}{2} = \dfrac{(17+25)8}{2} = 168 \text{ ft}^2\) \(\text{Area}_{Rectangle} = 15 \times 5 = 75 \text{ ft}^2\) \(\text{Area}_{Total} = 168 - 75 = 93 \text{ ft}^2\) Sta 4+57 \(\text{Top of trapezoid} = 30\) \(\text{Bottom of trapezoid} = 20\) \(\text{Area}_{Trapezoid} = \dfrac{(a+b)h}{2} = \dfrac{(30+20)10}{2} = 250 \text{ ft}^2\) \(\text{Area}_{Rectangle} = 16 \times 7 = 112 \text{ ft}^2\) \(\text{Area}_{Total} = 250 - 112 = 138 \text{ ft}^2\) \(V = L\left(\dfrac{A_1 + A_2}{2}\right)\) \(V = (457-235)\left(\dfrac{138+93}{2}\right) = 25641 \text{ ft}^3 = 950 \text{ yd}^3\)

Answer: C
Q36. A survey used to show directions and measurements of a proposed sewer mainline is a
intro
  • A) boundary survey
  • B) topographic survey
  • C) control survey
  • D) route survey
A route survey is a survey for determining the route, grades, etc., of linear projects like a railroad, highway, or pipe line.

Answer: D
Q37. The main advantage for using LiDAR instead of Photogrammetry for surveying is
gis
  • A) LiDAR data is far more accurate than Photogrammetry
  • B) LiDAR is much cheaper
  • C) LiDAR can be processed much faster than Photogrammetry
  • D) LiDAR can pick up points underneath the canopy of vegetation
Even through dense vegetation, some of the laser light pulses can get through tiny openings to provide a distance to the ground. This cannot be done with any other method, including Photogrammetry.

Answer: D
Q38. What type of land mark is the arrow pointing to?

level
  • A) cliff
  • B) ridge
  • C) stream
  • D) depression
The arrow is pointing to a stream. The characteristics are that the point of the "arrows" (contours crossing the stream) point upstream, and there is a line through the "points" representing the stream channel. This is a classic representation of a stream or river.

Answer: C
Q39. 1.345 rad to degrees, minutes, and seconds is
intro
  • A) 0°12'50"
  • B) 267°39'29"
  • C) 77°3'46"
  • D) 134°15'57"
\(\dfrac{1.345 \times 360^\circ}{2\pi} = 77^\circ3'46"\)

Answer: C
Q40. A large, open 50 mile by 60 mile area is to be surveyed. A few surveying options were considered however because of the size of the project, aerial surveying was selected. The designer needs very accurate data which will require the largest redundancies when considering lap percent. The options for the side lap are 30% or 35%. The options for the end lap are 60% or 65%. The photo dimensions are 9 inch x 9 inch and the required photo scale is 1:10000. What is the minimum number of flight lines needed to complete the survey?
gis
  • A) 55
  • B) 51
  • C) 88
  • D) 65
To get more redundant points, the side lap and end lap will need to be increased. Therefore 35% side lap will need to be used. \(Scale = \dfrac{1 \text{ in}}{10000 \text{ in}} = \dfrac{1"}{833.33'}\) \(\text{Distance between flight lines} = (1 - \text{sidelap}) \times W\) \(= (1-0.35) \times \dfrac{833.33'}{1"} \times 9"\) \(= 4875 \text{ ft/flight line}\) Number of flight lines: Typically to keep the number of flight lines to a minimum and increase efficiency, flights are along the long side of the project. So the number of flights are counted along the short side. \(50 \text{ miles} = 264{,}000 \text{ feet}\) \(\text{Number of flights} = \dfrac{\text{width}}{\text{distance between flight lines}}\) \(= \dfrac{264{,}000}{4875}\) \(= 54.15\) \(= 55 \text{ flight lines}\)

Answer: A
Q41. A natural depressed area is being considered for a proposed water storage area. The general contours and areas are shown in the table. What is the total existing capacity of this area?
Elevation (ft)260270280
Area (ft²)195618651692

area
  • A) 1.230 hectare-m
  • B) 0.104 hectare-m
  • C) 0.282 hectare-m
  • D) 0.121 hectare-m
Volume between contours 260 ft and 270 ft: \(\left(\dfrac{1956+1865}{2}\right)(270-260) = 19105 \text{ ft}^3\) Volume between contours 280 ft and 270 ft: \(\left(\dfrac{1865+1692}{2}\right)(280-270) = 17785 \text{ ft}^3\) Total Capacity Volume: \(\text{Total} = 19105 + 17785 = 36890 \text{ ft}^3\) \(36890 \text{ ft}^3 \times \dfrac{1 \text{ m}^3}{35.3134 \text{ ft}^3} \times \dfrac{1 \text{ hectare}}{10{,}000 \text{ m}^2} = 0.104 \text{ hectare-m}\)
Note: You can either convert units early in the problem or at the end. It is recommended to convert at the end to limit potential conversion errors, since you only need to convert the solution.

Answer: B
Q42. A flat 40-ft wide dirt road at an elevation of 176.18 ft is to be paved with 2 inches of asphalt. A flow line is to be constructed in the middle of the road with -2% cross slopes. To what elevation should the middle of the road be excavated to at sta 0+00?
constr
  • A) 175.78 ft
  • B) 175.61 ft
  • C) 176.58 ft
  • D) 175.95 ft
\(176.18 - 20(0.02) = 175.78 \text{ ft}\) \(175.78 - \dfrac{2}{12} = 175.61 \text{ ft}\)
Note: The top of the flowline is the finished surface elevation at the middle of the road. This is also the top of the 2" asphalt. If we were to add the 2" asphalt on top of this point, the slope to the edge of the road would no longer be 2% (it would be much lower). Therefore we must excavate 2" lower to account for the 2" asphalt.

Answer: B
Q43. The bearing of line QR is

trav
  • A) N30°21'22"W
  • B) S43°7'12"E
  • C) N43°7'12"W
  • D) S46°52'48"E
\(Distance\ PR = \sqrt{(6032.23-6324.23)^2 + (7825.41-5814.47)^2}\) \(Distance\ PR = 2032.03 \text{ ft}\) Law of Cosine \(r^2 = p^2 + q^2 - 2(p)(q)\cos(\angle PRQ)\) \(1350^2 = 1125^2 + 2032.03^2 - 2(2032.03)(1125)\cos(\angle PRQ)\) \(\angle PRQ = 38^\circ37'5"\) Find the x and y change to find angle PRS \(PS = 7825.41 - 5814.47 = 2010.94\) \(SR = 6324.23 - 6032.23 = 292\) \(\angle PRS = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2010.94}{292}\right)\) \(\angle PRS = 81^\circ44'17"\) \(\angle PRS - \angle PRQ = 81^\circ44'17" - 38^\circ37'5" = 43^\circ7'12"\) \(\text{bearing } RQ = N43^\circ7'12"W\) \(\text{bearing } QR = S43^\circ7'12"E\)
Student/instructor discussion:
S.M.Jul 05
I don't really understand how you found or decided on an "S" point? How did this come about?
S.S.Jul 09
I wasn't sure either.
Instructor Kirk TJul 12
Point "S" is a made up point in order to create a right triangle. We know its coordinates because we have the coordinates of point P and R. The northing of point S is the same as point P and the easting of point S is the same as point R. We created this point S in order to better visualize the bearing of line PR, which requires the departure and latitude from point P to R.

Alternatively, you can calculate the bearing of line PR using the coordinates of point P and point R without creating point S, by using the equation tan(theta)=departure/latitude. It's just used to visualize this.

Answer: B
Q44. In GIS, a TIN is
  1. an irregular tessellation
  2. a type of digital map illustrating specific subjects or topics
  3. a three dimensional surface formed from a series of irregularly shaped triangles
  4. a model that may be used as an alternative to the regular grid of a raster that comprises a digital elevation model (DEM) or digital terrain model (DTM)
  5. a triangulated irregular network
  6. a format for spatial data developed by the U.S. Bureau of Census

Igis
  • A) 1, 3, 4, and 5
  • B) 1, 2, 4, and 6
  • C) 3, 4, 5, and 6
  • D) 2 and 4
In GIS, a TIN is a triangulated irregular network. It is a representation of a continuous three dimensional surface built from triangular facets that connect heights, and non-overlapping triangles are connected along their edges. A TIN is also an alternative to the regular grid of a raster that comprises a digital elevation model (DEM). It has the advantage of allowing the representation of complex areas with densely spaced information, while sparse information can be used to represent simpler areas.
Note: Tessellation means the covering of a surface, often a plane, using one or more geometric shapes. Even if you did not now that, you should be able to deduce the answer choices down to one.

Answer: A

Q46. An offset stake is shown with information missing and cut off. A level is set up on the bench. What is the "X" value of the side slopes for the ditch?

constr
  • A) 4
  • B) 3
  • C) 3.5
  • D) 2.5
We must use the stake information and the leveling information to find the side slope ratio for the ditch. The height of the instrument (HI) is 5.3' because we know that the side slopes of the ditch are the same. \(\text{Height of ditch} = 8.2 - 5.3\) \(\text{Height of ditch} = 2.9\) To find the width of the side slopes, we must calculate the total length and subtract the known values. \(47.50 - 5 - 7.8 - 5 - 12.3 = 17.4\) \(\text{length of each side slope} = \dfrac{17.4}{2} = 8.7\) \(Grade = \dfrac{8.7}{2.9} = 3\)

Answer: B
Q47. Which of the following has the lowest accuracy for a vertical control network?
level
  • A) General area
  • B) Local control
  • C) Basic framework
  • D) Secondary network
From highest order (most accurate) to lowest order (least accurate) vertical control network: Basic framework is a uniformly distributed nationwide network of bench marks whose elevations are determined to the highest order of accuracy. It consists of nets A and B. In net A, adjacent level lines are ideally spaced an average of about 100 to 300 km apart using first-order class I standards; in net B the average separation is ideally about 50 to 100 km, and first-order class II standards are specified. Bench marks are placed intermittently along the level lines at convenient locations. Secondary network densifies the basic framework, especially in metropolitan areas and for large engineering projects. It is established to second-order class I standards. General area control consists of vertical control for local engineering, surveying, and mapping projects. It is established to second-order class II standards. Local control provides vertical references for minor engineering projects and small-scale topographic mapping. Bench marks in this category satisfy third-order standards.

Answer: B
Q48. What is the most precise method of finding vertical points?
level
  • A) indirect leveling
  • B) differential leveling
  • C) double-rodded leveling
  • D) three-wire leveling
Three-wire leveling is the most accurate as it averages the three lines through the scope instead of just using the middle cross hair. Differential leveling is a general term. Indirect leveling uses angles to find vertical and horizontal distance. All can be found in the glossary.
Student/instructor discussion:
Z.L.Mar 14
Does the three wire method is the same as the stadia method? Or three wire method is only the method to read the rod reading?
Instructor Kirk TMar 20
That is a good question. Three wire method is not the same as stadia method though it uses the same components of the top hair, middle hair, and bottom hair. In stadia, we use the hairs (more specifically the rod intercept in most cases) to calculate horizontal and vertical distances.

Three wire method, however, is specifically used at each reading individually, for which we average the three hair readings to calculate as accurate of a rod reading as possible.

Answer: D
Q49. In a closed traverse, the departures failed to close by -0.79' and the latitudes failed to close by +0.49'. The horizontal traverse distance is known to be 5649.2'. The bearing of the closing line from the misclosure end point is
trav
  • A) N31°48'34"W
  • B) S31°48'34"E
  • C) N58°11'26"W
  • D) S58°11'26"E
Start from the end point as noted in the problem. Don't worry about the negative sign since we can visually see where the bearing is located. Remember that the direction of the bearing line is A'A. A' is the end point of the misclosure and A is the starting point. \(\tan\left(\dfrac{0.79}{0.49}\right) = 58^\circ11'26"\) \(\text{Quadrant IV} = S58^\circ11'26"E\)

Answer: D
Q50. The central angle of a curve with an EC at station 16+23.89 is 27°11'7". The deflection angle to sta 15+84.03, a point along the curve with a radius of 950 feet, is
hc
  • A) 24°46'33"
  • B) 10°50'33"
  • C) 12°23'26"
  • D) 21°41'05"
In this case, you are essentially looking at a new curve from BC to 15+84.03. First find the BC of both curves. \(L_{large\ curve} = \dfrac{2\pi R I_{large\ curve}}{360^\circ}\) \(L_{large\ curve} = \dfrac{2\pi(950)(27^\circ11'7")}{360^\circ} = 450.75\) \(BC\ station = 1623.89 - 450.75 = 1173.14\) \(L_{from\ BC\ to\ 15\text{-}84.03} = \dfrac{2\pi R I_{from\ BC\ to\ 15\text{-}84.03}}{360^\circ}\) \(1584.03 - 1173.14 = \dfrac{2\pi(950)I'}{360}\) \(I' = 24^\circ46'53"\) \(\dfrac{I'}{2} = \text{deflection angle} = 12^\circ23'26"\)
Student/instructor discussion:
W.Z.May 14
Can we skip the calculation of BC STA? I mean can we look at the curve from 15+84.03 to EC (small curve) to get that small central angle instead of getting the I'? Because if we have that small central angle (which only requires one step to get that angle), we can get I' by "Delta minus small central angle," then just divide by 2 to get the answer. Am I correct?
Instructor Kirk TOct 02
It seems we missed this question. But yes absolutely that can be done! That is a great way of solving it. Here it is worked out as a shortcut:
Find the arc length from the point (sta 15+84.03) to the EC (sta 16+23.89): \(L_{small} = 1623.89 - 1584.03 = 39.86\) Find the small central angle for that arc: \(I_{small} = \dfrac{L_{small}\times 360^\circ}{2\pi R} = \dfrac{39.86\times 360^\circ}{2\pi(950)}\) \(I_{small} = 2^\circ24'14"\) Subtract from the total central angle and divide by 2 to get the deflection angle: \(\Delta - I_{small} = 27^\circ11'7" - 2^\circ24'14" = 24^\circ46'53"\) \(\text{deflection angle} = \dfrac{24^\circ46'53"}{2} = 12^\circ23'26"\)

Answer: C
Q51. What is the maximum radius that can be constructed for a horizontal curve between sta 278+38 on First St. and sta 118+99 on Second St. with the intersection of the tangents at the intersection of the First and Second street?

hc
  • A) 4855 ft
  • B) 5375 ft
  • C) 5161 ft
  • D) 5175 ft
Considering that the two tangents of a curve must be equal, we need to find what the maximum radius is that fits the tangents on both streets. The longer the radius, the longer the tangent should be. Therefore our constraint is the street that has the smaller tangent from the PI to the respective BC and EC stations given in the problem. The other stations in the diagram are extra information and not needed. \(\text{Tangent on First St.} = 392.35\text{ sta} - 278.38\text{ sta} = 113.97\text{ stations}\) \(\text{Tangent on Second St.} = 148.79\text{ sta} - 118.99\text{ sta} = 29.80\text{ stations}\) Therefore we select 29.80 sta as the tangent. I = Bearing of First St. minus bearing Second St. as shown in the figure. \(I = S82^\circ E - S22^\circ E = 60^\circ\) \(T = R_{max}\tan\dfrac{I}{2}\) \(R_{max} = \dfrac{T}{\tan\frac{I}{2}}\) \(R_{max} = \dfrac{29.80\text{ sta}}{\tan\frac{60^\circ}{2}} = 51.6151\text{ stations}\) \(R_{max} = 5161.51\text{ ft}\)

Answer: C
Q52. Line ABFG is the centerline finish grade of a roadway. The center point of curve BF is point H. The elevation at point B is 123.14 feet and the grade toward point F is +1.25%. An existing storm drain line EC intersects the road at point D. The invert elevation at point E is 105.97 feet and the grade toward point C is +1.0%. What is the difference in elevation between the road finish grade and the invert at point D?

constr
  • A) 13.54 feet
  • B) 4.98 feet
  • C) 4.92 feet
  • D) 6.14 feet
Find Curve BF Elevation: \(Radius\ of\ BF = \sqrt{(7436.61-8725.18)^2 + (13470.69-12653.45)^2} = 1525.87'\) \(Chord\ BD = \sqrt{(7436.61-7767.54)^2 + (13470.69-13841.40)^2} = 496.93'\) \(C_{BD} = 2R\sin\dfrac{I}{2}\) \(496.93 = 2(1525.87)\times\sin\dfrac{I}{2}\) \(I = 18.743^\circ\) \(L = \dfrac{2\pi RI}{360} = \dfrac{2\pi(1525.87)(18.743)}{360} = 499.15'\) \(Elevation_{D\ on\ curve} = L\times 1.25\% + 123.14 = 499.15\times 1.25\% + 123.14 = 129.38\) Find Line DE Elevation: \(Line\ DE = \sqrt{(9490.66-7767.54)^2 + (13186.97-13841.40)^2} = 1843.21'\) \(Elevation_{D\ on\ line} = DE\times 1.0\% + 105.97 = 1843.21\times 1.0\% + 105.97 = 124.40\) Elevation difference between the road FG and the invert at point D: \(129.38 - 124.40 = 4.98'\)
Note: FG means finished grade, which is the elevation at the top of the pavement or finished surface.

Answer: B
Q53. There is a construction project in the forest area. A 13-mile long route survey is requested by the client and you are the Project Engineer in charge of this work. Which of the following maps will you request before this survey?
intro
  • A) Parcel map
  • B) Aerial photograph
  • C) N.G.S map
  • D) Topographic map
A topographic map would be needed before a route survey to provide the existing topography. Aerial photograph will not work as this is a forest area. A parcel map simply breaks up a larger lot into smaller lots. And an NGS map is not descriptive enough to describe what that is, as NGS map does not mean anything.

Answer: D
Q54. A new roadway extension is proposed for a development. In order to extend the roadway leading into the development, a sewer line must be extended. The end of the existing roadway at the existing MH to the entrance of the development is 200 feet. The cut slope from the existing MH to MH2 is 3%. The slope of the roadway from MH2 to the entrance of the development must be 2% and the elevation of the invert at the entrance is 216.80. Assuming the pipe is laid flat, what is the excavation slope from MH2 to the project limits?

constr
  • A) 2%
  • B) 3%
  • C) 1.77%
  • D) 2.44%
"Pipe laid flat" implies the slope of the pipe is the same as the excavation slope. The surface slope (2%) and the cut slope (3%) do not have to be the same as long as soil cover requirements are satisfied. \(200 - 92 = 108 \text{ ft}\) \(108 \text{ feet} \times 0.03 = 3.24\) \(221.67 - 3.24 = 218.43 = \text{invert at MH2}\) \(218.43 - 216.80 = 1.63\) \(\dfrac{Rise}{Run} = Slope\) \(\dfrac{-1.63}{92} = 0.0177 = 1.77\%\)

Answer: C
Q55. The coordinates of the points of a horizontal curve are: BC N3500, E2000; EC N3653, E2479; PI N3700, E2200. What is the radius of the curve?
hc
  • A) 548.44 ft
  • B) 522.84 ft
  • C) 1065.93 ft
  • D) 308.55 ft
Find the chord length BC to EC: \(Chord = \sqrt{(3653-3500)^2 + (2479-2000)^2} = 502.84'\) Find the bearings of the tangents at BC and the chord. \(\text{Bearing of back tangent} = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{Departure}{Latitude}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2000-2200}{3500-3700}\right)\) \(PI \rightarrow BC\ bearing = S45^\circ W\) \(BC \rightarrow PI\ bearing = N45^\circ E\) \(\text{Bearing of chord starting @BC} = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2479-2000}{3653-3500}\right)\) \(\text{Bearing of chord starting @BC} = N72.2857^\circ E\) \(\dfrac{I}{2} = 72.2857 - 45 = 27.2857^\circ\) Use chord equation: \(C = 2R\sin\dfrac{I}{2}\) \(502.84 = 2R\sin 27.2857^\circ\) \(R = 548.44\)

Answer: A
